title: Bhishma's boon
hook: Shantanu gives his son power over his own death, and why Hindus still offer water to Bhishma
carry: he had no child, so hindus offer him water

segments.voice: Yesterday: one word, mother, a chariot ride to Hastinapura, and a son honoring his father's bride. Matru devo bhava: honor a mother as god.

Shantanu has just heard everything his son did at the fisherman's house: the throne given away, the lifelong vow, the bride brought home and called mother. Bhishma asked for nothing in return. He only told his father what he had done. Now his father gives him something anyway, and it's rare: a say over his own death.
screen: `THE THRONE, THE VOW, THE BRIDE.` → `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` → `DEATH ONLY WITH HIS LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The text says Shantanu was pleased by the hard thing his son had done. Death will not come near you while you wish to live, he tells him; it will come only with your leave. Tradition calls this icchamrityu, death at will. Look at the trade. The son gave away his future: a crown, a marriage, children of his own. The father answers with the one thing no one gets to choose, the hour of his own death. Remember it. Many years from now, lying on a bed of arrows, Bhishma will use this gift, waiting for the sun to turn north before he lets death come. But today's teaching is about the children he gave up. In Hindu tradition, the living care for the dead. Children and grandchildren offer water to their ancestors, a rite called tarpana, and food in the larger rite called shraddha. A man with no children has no one to make them. Bhishma chose that, for his father's happiness. And here's how the tradition answers him. On a day called Bhishma Ashtami, remembered as the day he finally let death come, many Hindus offer water in his name, the way they would for their own grandfather. He gave up having a family, so the whole tradition became his family. Readers still weigh the vow: some honor it as devotion to a father; some ask hard questions about a king who let his son pay that price. The Mahabharata holds both, and moves on to the bride. Her story begins long before this marriage.
screen: `ICCHAMRITYU: DEATH AT WILL.` · `HE GAVE UP CROWN, MARRIAGE, CHILDREN.` · `NO CHILDREN TO OFFER HIM WATER.` · `BHISHMA ASHTAMI.` · then, large: `HINDUS OFFER HIM WATER.`

segments.voice: In tarpana, many Hindus offer water from cupped hands, naming the people who came before them. If there's a glass of water near you, hold it. Bring to mind someone who gave something up so your life could go well: a parent, a grandparent, someone who was never really thanked. Say their name quietly, as a prayer if you pray, or simply as thanks. Then, when you can, pour a little onto a plant or the earth, the way tarpana gives water back.
Bhishma's vow. A son gave up his line for his father; his father gave him death at his own leave; and the tradition gives him the water no child could.
Your line: he had no child, so Hindus offer him water. Next, the bride's own story. See you tomorrow.
